items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Humberto could not speak very good english, but I would understand him and we became good friends.

ctx.x: Back in Paris, my regular handout became the Omnibus Café in the Place Pigalle, which was a one minute walk from the hotel I was staying at on rue Henri Monnier. Many French and Martinique musicians met on the square at Place Pigalle every evening around 6, which is known as the apertif hour. It was also where musicians were engaged for gigs the way it was at the Rhythm Club back home. I met some musicians I had known before the last war at Place Pigalle.

Django, his brother Joseph, Louis Vola ex-bassist of the quintet du Hot Club de France, Alix Combelle, André Ekyan and some Cubans, one named Raoul and Humberto Canto who played bongos and danced. Humberto could not speak very good english, but I would understand him and we became good friends. He was very folly fellow. There were also two Algerian fellows that I became quite friendly with. One was named Mohammed Hamida, but I called him "Monsieur Chemise" because he admired the shirts I wore. Chemise in french…

The other Algerian was called Pépé and he spoke good english. After a few times talking with Pépé, I figured I knew him well enough to ask him if he knew where I could get some gage. I was never an addict but I liked a little taste now and then and Pépé said he knew something. He asked me how much I wanted and as I didn't know how it was sold here, I figured that three thousand francs would get me a few sticks, so I told him to bring me enough for that amount.
